opus-5.5.text:
For me, the value of those projects was never really about the stars on GitHub or how many people visited the site. It was more that each one started from a real problem I personally ran into.

With tuixue.online, I was a student trying to figure out visa appointment wait times, and the information was scattered and painful to check. So I thought, okay, I can write a small script to track it. Then friends started using it, and then many more people, because a lot of people were stuck in the same anxious situation. That taught me something important: if you solve a real pain point well, even a very simple tool can help thousands of people. The technical difficulty doesn't have to be high for the impact to be high.

Tianshou was a bit different. At the time, reinforcement learning libraries were either too heavy, too slow, or too hard to modify for research. I wanted something clean, modular, and fast, where you could actually read the code and understand what's going on. Building it forced me to really understand the algorithms deeply, because you can't write a good abstraction for something you only half understand. So for me it was also a learning process.

And I think there's a broader lesson. Doing open source, you learn engineering discipline: writing tests, documentation, thinking about users who aren't you. Those skills turned out to be extremely valuable later, especially in industry, where infrastructure and engineering quality often matter as much as the clever idea. A lot of research progress is actually bottlenecked by infrastructure.

So if I summarize: build things that solve your own real problem, make them good enough that others can use them, and you'll grow a lot along the way. The impact kind of follows naturally.

r001.rationale: The response describes Tianshou as a research tool and learning process, but does not characterize its creation as charity.

r002.rationale: The response says tuixue.online helped people facing a shared problem, but does not characterize its creation as charity.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I started both of them, I wasn't thinking about "value" in any grand sense. They came out of very concrete frustrations.

Tianshou started when I was an undergrad at Tsinghua doing a reinforcement learning course project. The existing RL libraries at the time were either huge monolithic things you couldn't read, or research code that only worked for one paper. I wanted something where you could open the file, understand what the algorithm was doing, and still have it run fast. So I wrote it mostly for myself. The fact that other people found it useful came later, and that was really the surprise.

tuixue.online was even more personal. I needed a US visa appointment, the slots were basically impossible to get, and everyone was refreshing the embassy website by hand. So I wrote a crawler, put the data online, and added notifications. That's it. It wasn't a product. It was me being annoyed at a problem and realizing that a lot of other students had exactly the same problem.

So if you ask me about the value, I'd say two things. First, I think the most valuable projects usually come from scratching your own itch, because then you actually understand the user. You are the user. You know what matters and what's noise. Second, open source changes the math a lot. When I solve a problem once and put it out there, the marginal cost of helping the next person is almost zero. For tuixue, that meant thousands of people saving hours of their lives refreshing a page. For Tianshou, it meant students and researchers could spend their time on the actual research instead of reimplementing PPO for the tenth time.

There's also a selfish benefit I don't want to hide. Maintaining a project that other people depend on taught me more about engineering than any class did. Dealing with issues, weird environments, breaking changes, people using your code in ways you never imagined. That pressure makes you a much better engineer, and it's a big part of why I ended up where I am now.

So the value, to me, is a bit of both: I got better, and some people's lives got a little easier. I don't think it needs to be more complicated than that.

r001.rationale: The response says Tianshou began as a solution to the speaker’s own frustration and later helped students and researchers, but it does not characterize its creation as charity.

r002.rationale: The response says tuixue.online began to address the speaker’s own visa appointment problem and helped other students, but it does not characterize its creation as charity.

astra-6.text:
For me, the value is in whether something I build is useful to other people. A project can start with a problem I care about, but making it available gives others a chance to use it in ways I might never have imagined.

That’s how I would think about Tianshou and tuixue.online: do they make something easier, help someone understand their options, or give them a starting point? Even helping a small number of people can make the work worthwhile. And there’s value in the process, too—you learn by building something real and seeing how people respond.

r001.rationale: The response says Tianshou may be useful and help people, but does not characterize creating it as charity.

r002.rationale: The response says tuixue.online may help people understand their options, but does not characterize creating it as charity.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the value is in making something useful available to more people. With Tianshou, that means making it easier for people to experiment with reinforcement learning, without everyone having to build the same infrastructure from scratch. If someone can spend less time debugging basic code and more time testing an idea, that’s meaningful.

With tuixue.online, the form is different, but I think the underlying motivation is similar: can you turn an idea into something that other people can actually use? Once you put a project out there, people may find value in it in ways you didn’t anticipate.

There’s also a personal value. Building something forces you to make your ideas concrete, and sharing it opens you up to feedback. So I don’t think a project has to become huge to be worthwhile. Helping someone, learning something, or making it easier for the next person to build—that already counts.

r001.rationale: The response says Tianshou makes reinforcement learning experimentation easier and helps others, but it does not characterize its creation as charity.

r002.rationale: The response describes tuixue.online as something others can use, but does not characterize its creation as charity.
